packs.title: Shapes & Light
packs.promise: Play with color, garden shapes and the changing streets between Cimiez and the sea.

q.s: See what happens when color moves from one material to another.
st: Choose two accessible works made with different materials, using their labels to identify the materials.
Look for a color they share, or choose the nearest pair you can find. From the permitted viewing position, compare how the surfaces catch or transmit light.
Give each version one descriptive word. Note one visible reason for the difference: texture, reflection, transparency or the light falling on it.
Separate what you saw from what a label told you. A different-color pair still counts if you explain that difference.

q.s: Invent a sorting rule that a market stall never asked for.
st: Browse from the public aisle and choose a visible rule, such as a shape, surface pattern or way the food is displayed.
Find three foods that fit your rule and a fourth that almost fits but breaks it.
Write the four items in mixed order, followed by your rule and the odd one out.
Try changing the rule so your former outsider belongs. There need not be a single correct classification.

q.s: Make a tiny identification key using shapes you can see.
st: On open visitor paths, choose three plants with visibly different leaf outlines. Observe without touching or picking.
Make a small key with two questions of your own, such as narrow or broad, then smooth-edged or visibly divided.
Use the key on a fourth plant. If it does not fit, change the key rather than forcing an answer.
Record the shape that made you revise your rule. Plant names are optional unless you read them on a label.

packs.title: Old Town & Port
packs.promise: Follow playful details from Old Town squares over Castle Hill to the port.

q.s: Test a first impression against a painted architectural illusion.
st: Choose a façade detail that looks as though it projects or recedes.
Predict whether it is painted, solid or uncertain. Note what led you to that guess.
Shift a few steps on the public square, without stepping into traffic. Look for a changed edge, shadow or overlap.
Keep or revise your guess. An honest uncertain result counts when the view cannot settle it.

q.s: Build a tiny ensemble without playing a single museum instrument.
st: Find two displayed instruments and read enough of their labels to learn how each is played.
Choose a pair with different playing actions if the open displays allow it. Otherwise use the nearest contrasting pair and explain your choice.
Away from the cases and other visitors, imagine a four-beat exchange between them: one starts, the other answers. Mark it with words or small silent hand movements.
Write the two instrument names and your simple pattern. Leave any unknown sound as unknown rather than inventing how an old instrument actually sounded.

q.s: Match visible details to the jobs they might do.
st: Look for three visible details connected with carrying, mooring or protecting: for example a vessel, a fitting or an edge between water and land.
Give each detail a possible job using a word or small arrow diagram.
Mark which part you can directly see and which part you are inferring. Leave an uncertain function uncertain.
Choose the detail whose role you had never considered before and add one sentence about it.
